title: Cleopatra and the Moon
body: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing in 1969 than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza, which was built about 2,500 years before she was born.

title: Uganda’s big day
body: Uganda became independent from Britain on 9 October 1962. Every year the country marks Independence Day on that date.

title: Kasubi: a royal home of Buganda
body: The Kasubi Tombs in Kampala are the burial place of the Kabakas of Buganda. They became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001. The main building, made of reeds and bark cloth, was badly damaged by fire in 2010, and work to restore it followed.

title: Timbuktu: a city of books
body: In the 1300s to 1500s Timbuktu in Mali was a famous centre of learning. Scholars came from far away, and its libraries kept hundreds of thousands of manuscripts.

title: The first Olympic Games
body: Records say the ancient Olympic Games began in Greece in 776 BC. They were held every four years, in honour of the god Zeus.

title: Mansa Musa and the gold
body: In 1324 Mansa Musa, the ruler of Mali, travelled to Mecca with so much gold that it is said to have lowered the price of gold in Cairo for years. He is often called one of the richest people in history.

title: The wheel is a young idea
body: People farmed for thousands of years before anyone made a wheel. Some of the oldest evidence of wheels comes from Mesopotamia about 5,500 years ago, where potters used them.

title: Great Zimbabwe
body: Great Zimbabwe was a large stone city built between about the 1100s and 1400s. The name means “stone houses”, and the modern country of Zimbabwe took its name from it.

title: The printing press
body: In the 1450s Johannes Gutenberg built a printing press with movable metal letters in Germany. Books became cheaper and ideas spread far faster.

title: Uganda’s nickname
body: Winston Churchill visited Uganda in 1907 and called it “the Pearl of Africa” because of its beauty and rich wildlife. The nickname has stuck.

title: The Nile civilisation
body: Ancient Egypt grew along the Nile because the yearly flood left rich soil on the land. The Egyptians counted a 365-day year, which is the base of our calendar.
